content: 1. Meta-analyses were conducted using either random-effects or fixed-effects models, depending on the heterogeneity of effect sizes. Hedge’s g correction factor was applied to adjust for small sample sizes. Thirteen trials were included in the meta-analysis. 2. Concurrent strength and endurance training (referred to as concurrent training) was found to improve health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and cardiopulmonary status in HIV-infected patients. However, it did not significantly affect muscle mass. 3. The effects on strength were more pronounced in studies with higher methodological quality and in trials with longer durations of resistance training (RT) and highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). 4. The systematic review by Gomes Neto et al. (2013) aimed to evaluate the impact of concurrent training on HRQOL and cardiopulmonary status in HIV-infected patients through randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The findings suggested that concurrent training is safe and potentially beneficial for medically stable adults living with HIV, with a non-adherence rate of 16%. 5. Exercise interventions, particularly aerobic exercise (AE) and progressive resistance exercise (PRE), were shown to improve body composition, strength, and certain metabolic parameters in people living with HIV (PLWH). However, the combination of AE and PRE did not demonstrate additional benefits compared to each modality alone. 6. A systematic review by Fillipas et al. (2010) highlighted that aerobic exercise reduced adiposity and improved lipid profiles, while resistance training increased body weight and limb girth. Larger, higher-quality trials are needed to better understand the effects of exercise on metabolic outcomes such as lipids, glucose, and bone density in PLWH. 7. Exercise was found to reduce depressive symptoms and anxiety in PLWH, as demonstrated in a meta-analysis by Heissel et al. (2019). Subgroup analyses revealed that supervised exercise and higher-quality studies yielded more significant improvements. However, further research is required to confirm these findings. 8. A systematic review by Quiles et al. (2019) examined the effects of exercise on lipid profiles and blood glucose levels in PLWH. Improvements were observed in blood glucose, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and total cholesterol, depending on the type of exercise performed. Methodological limitations and variability in exercise protocols warrant cautious interpretation of these results. 9. Resistance training alone or combined with aerobic exercise (AERT) was shown to improve muscle strength in PLWH, particularly in studies with low risk of bias and professional supervision. Additionally, exercise was associated with reduced levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6), a marker of inflammation. 10. A systematic review by Nosrat et al. (2017) found that both aerobic and resistance exercise positively impacted mental health outcomes in PLWH. However, limitations such as high attrition rates, small sample sizes, and poor study designs were noted. Future studies should include more diverse populations, such as women, older adults, and transgender individuals. 11. Gomes Neto et al. (2013) conducted a systematic review to evaluate the effects of different types of therapeutic exercise on physiological and functional outcomes in patients with HIV. Resistance training improved body composition and muscle strength, while aerobic exercise enhanced aerobic capacity and body composition. Concurrent training yielded significant improvements across all evaluated outcomes, particularly with moderate intensity and longer durations. 12. A systematic review by Lopez et al. (2015) summarized the effects of aerobic or resistance training, as well as combined aerobic and resistance exercise training (CARET), on disease progression, fitness, physical functioning, mental health, and quality of life (QOL) in PLWH receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). Aerobic exercise improved aerobic capacity, QOL, and depressive symptoms, while resistance training enhanced strength. CARET demonstrated benefits across multiple domains.
